title: Rooted in the humble
hookLine: the high is rooted in the low; nobility rests on humility (Tao Te Ching 39)

cards: In chapter thirty-nine of the Tao Te Ching, kings call themselves by lowly names. The chapter says princes and rulers call themselves the orphaned, the lonely, the unworthy. Not the mighty.
Not the glorious. The ones at the very top of the ladder choose names from the very bottom of it. Odd, until you see what the chapter is building.
It starts in the sky and works its way down to the ground, and it ends with a plain stone. By tradition it belongs to the book's part on de, and it's about where height comes from.

teach.h: HEAVEN CLEAR, EARTH STEADY, BY THE ONE.
teach.b: First, the One. The chapter opens with a list of things that have attained the One, which Legge explains as the Tao. Heaven, by it, is clear.

Earth, by it, is steady. Spirits have their power from it, valleys are full, living things are alive, and rulers set the pattern for everyone else. Each has its best quality from something it didn't make.
Second, without it. The chapter runs the list again in reverse.
Without what makes it clear, heaven would crack. Without what makes it steady, earth would shake. Valleys would run dry, living things would perish, rulers would fall.
Nothing on the list holds itself up. Third, the root.

teach.h: THE HIGH STANDS ON THE LOW.
teach.b: Here's the heart of it, paraphrased: the noble takes the lowly as its root, and the high takes the low as its foundation. That's why kings, the chapter says, call themselves orphaned, lonely, unworthy.
They're naming what they stand on. Fourth, the stone. The chapter ends with two materials.
It doesn't want to glitter like jade.
It would rather be plain and rough, like an ordinary stone.

Outside the palace, the high things in a life stand on something low. The person at the top of a company stands on people who clean the building at night. A good dinner stands on someone washing pans.
A healthy body stands on sleep and water and feet. The chapter's kings remember that out loud, in their own names.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-nine as a reminder that anything high depends on what is low, and practice humility by honoring plain work and the people who do it.

games.q: what does “rooted in the humble” mean?
o: humble people are meant to stay low forever
the high stands on the low as its foundation
kings should hide their wealth from the people

p: takes the lowly as its root

games.q: you're a ruler, putting your name on a letter to your people. how does chapter thirty-nine say rulers name themselves?
o: the orphaned, the lonely, the unworthy.
games.why: the chapter says rulers take humble names, because the high takes the low as its foundation.

practice: Feel what's holding you up right now: the floor, the chair, the ground under the building. Rest your weight on it, and breathe.
Then bring to mind one low, unglamorous job that keeps your days standing, and the hands, yours or someone else's, that do it.
